https://www.politico.eu/article/donald-t.text: MADRID — If Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez had hoped tensions with Morocco would blow over after this summer’s influx of more than 70,000 migrants into the Spanish exclave of Ceuta in North Africa, those hopes were dashed on Monday evening. At a carefully choreographed religious ceremony at the royal palace in Rabat, with King Mohammed VI in attendance, Morocco’s Minister of Islamic Affairs Ahmed Toufiq described a 15th-century imam as a symbol for Moroccans “to liberate the occupied cities.” For Sánchez’s beleaguered Socialist government, Toufiq’s menacing reference to Spain’s autonomous cities of Ceuta and Melilla on the African coast — home to some 170,000 mainly Spanish citizens — forms part of a worrying pattern of increasingly assertive claims from Rabat. Advertisement Advertisement Only last week, Spain’s foreign ministry had to push back against a call from Morocco’s Justice Minister, Abdellatif Ouahbi, for Madrid and Rabat to discuss the future of the two cities, citing Morocco’s historic and geographical “right” to them. Facing a general election in the coming months and already floundering under a welter of corruption scandals in his party, Sánchez is desperate to avoid a showdown with Morocco — a country with which Madrid needs to maintain smooth relations because of its vital importance as a partner on trade, migration and fighting drug trafficking. Since the beginning of the crisis in Ceuta, Sánchez has sought to avoid blaming King Mohammed’s operatives, instead pointing the finger at smuggling networks and misleading social media campaigns for the migrant influx. His Migration Minister Elma Saiz has even hailed Morocco as “a reliable partner, a loyal partner.” Blaming Morocco But that diplomatic tone with Rabat is playing badly with the rest of Spain’s parties. Many politicians complain that Rabat withdrew border guards before the surge across the border. Alberto Núñez Feijóo, leader of the conservative People’s Party (PP), who is the current favorite to succeed Sánchez as prime minister, said: “It turns out that [Sánchez] behaves more like a subject of Morocco than a prime minister of Spain.” He then insisted Spain could not be subject to “blackmail and threats” from its neighbor across the Mediterranean. Advertisement Advertisement The leader of the far-right Vox party, Santiago Abascal, has gone further, describing the events in Ceuta as “an act of war promoted by Morocco.” And it is not just parties on the right blaming Morocco. The far-left Podemos used similar language to Vox, accusing Rabat of waging “a hostile act of hybrid war.” Sumar, the junior partner in Sánchez’s left-wing government, lodged a request in parliament that Morocco’s status as co-host of the 2030 World Cup, alongside Spain and Portugal, should be withdrawn because of its alleged role in the Ceuta crisis. The Trump factor The fear among numerous observers in Spain is that King Mohammed is a close strategic ally of U.S. President Donald Trump, who could be out to show he can be useful to Washington and to Israel by stirring up trouble for Sánchez. The Spanish prime minister has certainly made himself a potential target for MAGA and the Israeli administration. He has opposed Trump over the war in Iran, denying U.S. forces the use of Spanish bases, and has condemned Israel’s actions in Gaza as “genocide.” King Mohammed, by contrast, is making every effort to stay in Trump’s good books, and has good relations with Israel. The Moroccan king joined the U.S. president’s Gaza-related Board of Peace and even named a major highway after Trump over the summer. Advertisement Advertisement Antonio Maíllo, leader of the United Left (IU) party, a junior partner in Sánchez’s coalition, said the “United States-Israel-Morocco alliance … has one objective: to destabilize the [Spanish] government.” Morocco itself denies any such motivations and — like S´ánchez — blames the migrant surge on online disinformation. Riccardo Fabiani, North Africa project director at the International Crisis Group, believed it was reasonable to interpret the events in Ceuta as a message from Morocco “to Israel and the U.S. to show them: ‘Look, we’ve done what you implicitly told us to do, we’ve humiliated Spain.” “The manipulation of migration is something that Morocco is known to have used in the past,” Fabiani also noted. For Spaniards, the idea that Morocco could engineer a situation to annex Ceuta and Melilla is far from theoretical speculation. Many still remember Morocco’s 1975 “Green March,” an operation mobilizing tens of thousands of civilians to force Madrid to hand over the territory of Spanish Sahara. Prickly relationship Jorge Dezcallar, a former Spanish ambassador to Morocco and former head of the Spanish intelligence service, warned that Sánchez’s willingness to accommodate Morocco was backfiring. “Rabat confuses concessions with weakness and even more so when the concessions are constant,” he said. Advertisement Advertisement Spain’s economy is 10 times bigger than Morocco’s, and the European country was once a colonial overlord there. But, as Jacob Mundy, associate professor of peace and conflict studies at Colgate University, points out, Spain relies on its neighbor for cooperation in a number of areas beyond migration, including anti-narcotics and anti-terrorism operations. “Spain and Morocco have been at war with each other on and off for centuries and yet they have these profoundly deep, commercial, security and other kinds of relationships,” he said. “You’d think: Spain’s the bigger economy and so on, it’s going to be the one in charge, and yet Morocco has found ways to have the upper hand to some degree,” he added, underlining the “prickliness” that Madrid often encounters when dealing with Rabat. For Spain, the idea that Morocco could engineer a situation to annex Ceuta and Melilla is far from theoretical speculation. | Adri Salido/Getty Images Morocco’s alleged manipulation of migratory flows into Ceuta and Melilla is one such example, as well as periodically preventing Spanish fishing fleets from accessing its waters. The perception that Sánchez has been soft on Morocco was fueled by his government’s decision, in 2022, to end nearly five decades of Spanish neutrality on Western Sahara by backing Rabat’s proposal that the territory should come under its control. That was seen as an effort by Madrid to secure once and for all its neighbor’s cooperation on migration and prevent repeats of May 2021, when Morocco allowed around 10,000 people to cross into Ceuta in the space of a few hours. Advertisement Advertisement The concern for Madrid now is that its pivot on Western Sahara four years ago may not have had the desired effect. Having made progress on its claims to the territory, Morocco instead appears to have been emboldened to broach the question of Ceuta and Melilla. “From Morocco’s perspective Ceuta and Melilla have always been an open issue, they have always referred to those two territories as occupied,” said Fabiani, who said that recent remarks from U.S. and and Israeli officials broaching the issue made it “low-hanging fruit” for the Moroccans. He argued that, having made such a bold move to placate Morocco on Western Sahara, Sánchez does not feel he can afford to row back to a more hardline stance. In the meantime, Morocco’s leadership appears to be closely following the criticism the Spanish government is facing over its handling of this thorny bilateral relationship. It also seems determined to ensure that, with a general election due within a year, Spain’s next prime minister, widely expected to be Feijóo, follows this government’s line of engagement. Le360, a publication seen as close to the royal household, stated: “Cooperation with Morocco is not a specific concession on the part of Pedro Sánchez, but rather a structural necessity for any Spanish government, including one led by Feijóo.” But with Feij´óo slamming Sánchez’s deference to Morocco — and potentially governing with hardliners in Vox — it may be a miscalculation from Rabat that the next government will take so diplomatic an approach. Read more A body has been found in the search for a missing British teenager who went missing while hiking in Romania . George Smyth, a geology university student from Bristol , went missing in November last year trying to hike to Bran , the village known for its castle suggested to be the home of Dracula. Avon and Somerset Police said a body has been found in the Bucegi Mountain region of the country, which is believed to be that of Mr Smyth, although formal identification has yet to take place. Officers have informed Mr Smyth’s family of the development and are being supported by a family liaison officer. They shared a statement expressing gratitude to those who have supported the search for Mr Smyth and asked for privacy and time to grieve and process what has happened. Mr Smyth’s family said: “We are all devastated by George’s death. He was the best of us and is deeply missed by his younger brothers, family and friends. open image in gallery The operation was hindered by adverse weather ( Salvamont Brașov ) “We want to thank Salvamont Mountain Rescue, who have worked tirelessly since November searching for George; despite very difficult and often dangerous conditions. They are an amazing team, and have remained in constant communication, helping us greatly throughout this awful time. “We would also like to thank Avon and Somerset Police and University of Bristol, who have gone above and beyond to try and find George, and to support us as a family. “Although this latest news is incredibly painful, the torture of waiting is finally over, so we can now focus on bringing George home and saying goodbye. We would appreciate privacy while we continue to come to terms with this loss.” The teenager went missing on a hike near Bran Castle last year after he set off from the Poiana Brasov neighbourhood last November, rescuers said. The teenager reached Tiganesti Valley, where he made the call to rescue teams. Mountain rescuers, thermal imaging cameras, sniffer dogs, and a Black Hawk helicopter were mobilised as part of the operation, which was hindered by adverse weather with snow reaching more than 2m deep. Forensic enquiries are set to take place in order to confirm the identity of the body before the deceased will return to Bristol. https://www.dw.com/en/russia-s-hybrid-at.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5KZNu Ukrainian Antonov cargo planes like this one take off from Leipzig, carrying military supplies for Ukraine Image: Hendrik Schmidt/dpa/picture alliance Advertisement Fortunately, nothing bad happened this time around. Had the attack succeeded, however, who knows what the consequences might have been: On the evening of August 4 , a drone outfitted with explosives and a detonation device was discovered near Ukrainian cargo planes in the security area of Leipzig/Halle Airport. The airport serves as a hub for military aid to Ukraine . The German government hesitated for a long time before publicly holding Russia responsible . But now it has announced its findings. On Tuesday, Federal Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt told reporters that the methods used in the attempted attack were consistent with those seen in other Russian hybrid operations, citing the drone's construction, various components, explosives and detonation technology. He noted that the attack had been planned with a "high degree of technical expertise and considerable organizational effort." In late August, Chancellor Friedrich Merz said of the incident: "The federal government will make the perpetrators of hybrid attacks pay a price. They will pay for this." At the time, he did not mention Russia by name. And even now, Merz himself has not commented on the matter. However, the price Russia will have to pay is relatively small. The Russian House cultural institute in Berlin is being shut down amid suspicions that it is serving as a cover for espionage. The Russian Consulate General in Bonn is also being closed. What's more, entry requirements for Russian citizens are set to be tightened, and Germany also plans to take tougher action against the Russian "shadow fleet" — the network of ships ​accused of circumventing fuel sanctions. Exactly how and when remains unclear, however. Mixed reactions to Germany's measures For the environmentalist Green Party in the Bundestag , however, the government's response was lacking. "The federal government's analysis came a bit late, and the steps it's taking aren't enough for me," said Sara Nanni, the Greens' security policy spokesperson, in a DW interview. "I don't think anyone in Moscow is afraid or giving it a second thought right now." As an example, she said Germany should be taking tougher action against the Russian shadow fleet. This would be necessary to "stop the flow of money to the Russian war machine," she said. Acts of sabotage linked to Russia surge in Europe To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Roderich Kiesewetter, security expert with Chancellor Merz' center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU), is also dissatisfied. In the Handelsblatt newspaper, he called for the delivery of Taurus cruise missiles to Ukraine — and for the activation of Article 4 of the NATO Treaty, which requires allies to engage into consultations in the event of an external threat. He urged the German government to abandon "the politically convenient path of appeasement." However, wouldn't responding more assertively, as Kiesewetter has demanded, risk provoking a military confrontation with Russia, especially given that Russia has flatly denied responsibility for the Leipzig incident? On Tuesday, Russian President Vladimir Putin called the German sanctions against his country a "serious mistake" and accused Germany of fabricating evidence. The Foreign Ministry in Moscow announced that it would take countermeasures. Foreign Minister Wadephul sees Germany as a target Once again, the question of whether Germany is already at war with Russia is being raised — and this time with even greater urgency. But the federal government has unequivocally denied it. "We are not at war, but we are the daily target of hybrid warfare," said Interior Minister Dobrindt on Tuesday, after he blamed Russia for the failed attack. Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul told German public broadcaster ARD that Germany is not at war but is a Russian "war target." A year ago, in September 2025, Chancellor Merz said — though without naming Russia: "We are not at war, but we are no longer at peace either." This came against the backdrop of increasing attacks on data networks, critical infrastructure and hybrid threats. Security expert Sönke Marahrens from the University of Kiel offered a more nuanced answer: "No, Germany is not at war at the moment. We are facing hybrid activities by other countries, but we are not at war." In Western countries, he noted, declarations of war are regulated by law. And in Germany, according to the constitution, the Bundestag must declare that the country is at war, and that applies only after a physical attack. "Nothing currently meets that definition," he said. Ex-Lithuanian FM: 'We are on a trajectory of escalation' To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video However, the Green Party's Nanni fears Russia will continue to escalate the situation. "We are not yet at war with Russia, but Russia appears to be preparing for a war not only against Ukraine but against all of Europe," she said, calling the incident in Leipzig an "attempted terrorist act." Not at war with Russia From a legal standpoint, too, Germany is not at war with Russia. No declaration of war has been made, no recognized armed conflict exists, and no collective defense obligation has been invoked under NATO's Article 5 . Furthermore, consultations among NATO members, which must take place before a collective defense obligation can be invoked, have not been scheduled under Article 4. But things look different when it comes to hybrid warfare, which is not as precisely defined. Numerous security experts have argued that Russia is already waging just such a hybrid war against Western nations. This refers to attacks on infrastructure, cyberattacks, disinformation and traditional espionage. However, the line between hybrid war and an open act of war are blurry. Marahrens believes Russia is using hybrid actions — such as the one in Leipzig — to advance its strategic interests in Germany, the second-most important supporter of Ukraine after the US. Had the attack at the airport been successful, it would have relieved pressure on the Russian front, Marahrens said. He went on to say that "if Russia succeeds in convincing the German public not to support these political decisions [to support Ukraine], that would also directly reduce the pressure on the front lines." AfD opposes further military support for Ukraine The state election on Sunday in Saxony-Anhalt is one current example of Russian strategic interests. Many observers believe that this election is the most important in Germany in decades. The key question is whether the Alternative for Germany (AfD) — which is classified as far right by the Office for the Protection of the Constitution, Germany's domestic intelligence agency — will secure an absolute majority and, for the first time, govern a German state. The AfD opposes further military support for Ukraine and would like to normalize relations with Russia. This resonates with many in eastern Germany, where the war in Ukraine is seen by many as none of Germany's business, and where there is a feeling that too much money has already been sent to Ukraine. What if Germany's far-right AfD party wins in Saxony-Anhalt? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video This is why the federal government — composed of the conservative CDU/CSU bloc and the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) — is being careful about stepping up its rhetoric, as doing so could potentially help the AfD secure an absolute majority in Saxony-Anhalt. On the other hand, it can hardly afford to place the blame for the events in Leipzig on Russia while also responding in only a relatively mild manner. This dilemma may also be the reason why Chancellor Merz has so far refrained from speaking out to blame Russia. This article was originally written in German. By JAMES BROOKS and KIRSTEN GRIESHABER COPENHAGEN, Denmark (AP) — Denmark’s government was cautiously optimistic on Saturday following Donald Trump’s announcement of a deal on Greenland to bolster U.S. military presence there but keep the island under Danish control, after months of threats by the U.S. president to seize the semiautonomous territory of a NATO ally . The Arctic island’s top leaders echoed that stance and said the deal, which has not yet been made public, was long in coming. U.S., Greenlandic and Danish officials had quietly negotiated for months behind the scenes, searching for solutions to address some of Trump’s security concerns about the territory of roughly 56,000 residents. With the announcement of the pact, Trump is able to tout a foreign policy achievement ahead of the midterm elections in the United States. Trump said Friday that the agreement would give the U.S. “permanent control over security, and all other needs, in Greenland, completely addressing ALL of our many U.S. concerns.” Denmark and the U.S. already have a long-standing security agreement that allows the U.S. to deploy forces in Greenland, and it was not immediately clear how this deal would be different from that. “I think it’s obvious that we can expect more bases in Greenland. But it’s important to say that if we look in the past, especially during the Cold War, the U.S. had immense military presence in Greenland,” said Marc Jacobsen, an associate professor at the Royal Danish Defense College and the head of research at the Center for Arctic Security Studies. He said it was a win for Trump. “It’s important for him to show that he’s a good businessman, that he kind of forced the pressure on Denmark and Greenland into something new.” The deal is expected to be signed at the UN After Trump’s announcement, the office of Denmark’s Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said the deal will be signed next week at the United Nations General Assembly. Parliamentary action was still needed by the Danish and Greenlandic governments before it can be enforced, she added. “Next week could be a good week … for Greenland, Denmark, and the United States alike,” Danish Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen wrote on Instagram on Saturday morning. “A period of uncertainty will hopefully be replaced by a binding agreement that strengthens security in the Arctic and the North Atlantic — and thus also our shared security within NATO and Europe,” he added. Greenland’s government leader Jens-Frederik Nielsen said the deal would benefit “not only our collective security, but also the continued development here in the country.” The island’s foreign minister, Múte B. Egede, said he was pleased “we now have an agreement within reach.” “I’m pleased that we finally have an end product within reach,” he told Denmark’s TV2 broadcaster. “It’s about time.” Adm. Giuseppe Cavo Dragone, chair of the NATO Military Committee, said later Saturday in the Danish capital that the agreement was “very, very welcome,” without commenting on it further. Trump said that with the agreement, the U.S. would “immediately” begin the process of developing a larger military presence on the mineral-rich Danish territory. The U.S. had held several bases and installations on Greenland through the Cold War, before dialing back its presence. It still operates the remote Pituffik Space Base in northwestern Greenland, built after the U.S. and Denmark signed the Defense of Greenland Treaty in 1951. The base supports missile warning, missile defense and space surveillance operations for the U.S. and NATO. Few details about the deal are known so far A U.S. State Department official said the agreement bans any non-NATO base in Greenland, limits adversaries from being able to make investments in Greenland, and guarantees that China and Russia cannot have a base on the island. The official was not authorized to comment publicly and spoke on condition of anonymity. Denmark and Greenland did not explicitly confirm any of the specifics in Trump’s statements, nor did they provide more details. After his return to the White House, Trump had called on Denmark to sell the island to the U.S., while insisting Greenland is crucial for U.S. security . He pointedly wouldn’t rule out taking the island by military force , even though Denmark is a NATO ally of the U.S. Denmark and Greenland repeatedly said the island is not for sale and condemned reports of the U.S. gathering intelligence there. The U.S. push for Greenland was also fiercely opposed by Russia and much of Europe. Greenland grassroots pro-sovereignty activist Orla Joelsen wrote on X that “our fight against Trump’s ambition to take over Greenland has been won.” “The new agreement explicitly recognizes the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom of Denmark and the Greenlandic people’s right to self-determination,” the activist added. Ulrik Pram Gad, a senior researcher and Arctic security expert at the Danish Institute for International Studies, said that Trump tries to sell it as a win. “He obviously didn’t get in this agreement what he originally set out to have — that is sovereign control over all of Greenland as a part of the United States.” Relief that a deal seems close In Denmark, many expressed relief that a deal with the U.S. seemed close. Michael Burgaard from Gentofte, north of Copenhagen, was hopeful the crisis was over “because just a fortnight ago, Donald Trump posted this map showing Greenland … as part of the U.S.” “We were kind of worried that he would take all of Greenland by force,” added the 56-year-old telecommunications worker. “So, the fact that we can settle this in a diplomatic way … I think it’s good.” Michael Frees, a 51-year-old high school teacher in Copenhagen, said he thinks the agreement is “the most realistic solution for us right now.” “We are a small nation and of course we have to cooperate with bigger countries and also the European Union,” he said. ___ Grieshaber reported from Berlin. Associated Press writer Kostya Manenkov in Tallinn, Estonia, contributed to this report. https://economictimes.indiatimes.com/new.text: Moscow: A fire broke out on a Liberian-registered oil tanker manned entirely by an Indian crew off the Russian Black Sea coastline following a Ukrainian drone strike, as stated by the Russian Transport Ministry.According to the ministry, the vessel was targeted by naval drones , which subsequently ignited crude oil within the Black Sea. The blaze raged with such intensity that emergency responders were initially unable to suppress the flames.The Russian Transport Ministry stated that firefighters would attempt to extinguish the fire once its severity subsided.Track latest RBI repo rate decisions hereAll 23 crew members were successfully evacuated following the assault, the ministry confirmed.The event transpired close to Sochi, a prominent Russian Black Sea resort destination with a population approaching 500,000.Footage shared across social media platforms captured intense orange flames blazing over the water, accompanied by a dense plume of black smoke billowing near Sochi.This tanker strike occurred a day after a separate vessel, the commercial ship MV ROYAD MAMMADOV, burned and sank off the Romanian coast in an incident resulting in two foreign fatalities and injuries to crew members, including three Indian nationals.Reacting to the escalation, India condemned the attack and reiterated its call for dialogue and diplomacy to end ongoing conflicts. The Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) confirmed that the injured crew members had been rescued by Romanian authorities and were receiving medical attention, while expressing gratitude for Bucharest's swift action. Indian Ambassador to Romania Manoj Mohapatra also visited the three Indian nationals receiving treatment at Constanța County Hospital to assure them of continued assistance.The MEA voiced grave concern over continued threats to commercial shipping, noting that such targeting severely undermines global commerce and the welfare of people worldwide, while highlighting India's role in co-launching the Group of Friends on Safety and Security of Shipping and Seafarers at the United Nations. External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar had similarly raised alarms over attacks on commercial vessels during his UN General Assembly address the previous week.Also read: 11 Indians injured as projectile hits vessel near Strait of HormuzCommercial maritime traffic across the Black Sea has faced escalating assaults since the onset of the Russia-Ukraine conflict in 2022, with both governments repeatedly targeting ships and marine infrastructure.Over recent days, Moscow has struck grain carriers transporting Ukrainian agricultural products close to Romania, an EU member state.Conversely, Kyiv maintains that its targeting of Russian petroleum infrastructure constitutes a legitimate response to nightly aerial bombardments hitting Ukrainian urban centres.Both belligerents have pledged to intensify their military operations in recent weeks, heightening anxieties regarding maritime security for commercial vessels navigating the Black Sea.Furthermore, Moscow has stepped up strikes against vital bridges in Kyiv and deployed daytime drone raids directed at the capital, introducing a new strategy that has triggered significant disruption and traffic congestion.The most recent tanker fire has further highlighted the persistent dangers confronting commercial shipping as hostilities persist.
